docs.title: Wyngthon Documentation
docs.text: Wyngthon is an asyncio-based Python library designed for interacting with the Wyng API. It lets you use your own account to write a wide range of bots and scripts for Wyng.

docs.title: Why Wyngthon?
docs.text:
• Simplicity: A simple, readable API for interacting with Wyng
  • Performance: asyncio support for concurrent operations
  • Rich features: Send messages, files and photos, and manage conversations
  • Event support: A powerful event system for automatic replies
  • Security: Secure storage of sessions and credentials

docs.title: send_message

async def send_message(entity, message=None, *, parse_mode=None, 
                       link_preview=None, file=None, force_document=None, 
                       clear_draft=None, background=None, 
                       supports_streaming=None, schedule=None, 
                       noforwards=None, comment_to=None, 
                       reply_to=None, top_msg_id=None)

Parameters:

  • entity: the message destination (username, phone number, chat ID)
  • message: the message text
  • parse_mode: the parse mode (markdown/html)
  • link_preview: whether to show a link preview
  • file: a file to send
  • reply_to: reply to a specific message

Example:

await client.send_message('username', 'Hello!')
await client.send_message('me', 'Message with **bold**')
await client.send_message('me', 'https://example.com', link_preview=False)

docs.title: What is FloodWaitError?
docs.text:
It is an error that occurs when you send requests too quickly. You need to wait:

from wyngthon.errors import FloodWaitError

try:
    await client.send_message('username', 'Hello!')
except FloodWaitError as e:
    print(f'Wait {e.seconds} seconds')

docs.title: What is PeerFloodError?
docs.text:
It is an error that occurs when you have reached the message-sending limit:

from wyngthon.errors import PeerFloodError

try:
    await client.send_message('username', 'Hello!')
except PeerFloodError:
    print('Message sending limit reached. Please wait.')

docs.title: How do I handle errors?
docs.text:
from wyngthon.errors import RPCError, FloodWaitError, PeerFloodError

async def safe_send(client, entity, message):
    try:
        await client.send_message(entity, message)
        return True
    except FloodWaitError as e:
        import asyncio
        await asyncio.sleep(e.seconds)
        return True
    except PeerFloodError:
        print('Message sending limit reached')
        return False
    except RPCError as e:
        print(f'Error: {e}')
        return False

docs.title: How do I run multiple clients at the same time?
docs.text:
import asyncio
from wyngthon import WyngClient

async def run_client(name, api_id, api_hash):
    client = WyngClient(name, api_id, api_hash)
    await client.start()
    await client.run_until_disconnected()

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(
        run_client('client1', api_id1, api_hash1),
        run_client('client2', api_id2, api_hash2)
    )

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Installation and Setup
docs.text: A guide to installing Wyngthon and configuring your development environment.

docs.title: Installing Python
docs.text:
Wyngthon is a Python library, so you first need to download and install Python from python.org (version 3.8 or higher is recommended).

Note

After installing Python, upgrade pip to the latest version:

python3 -m pip install --upgrade pip

docs.title: Installing the Library
docs.text:
To install Wyngthon, run the following command:

python3 -m pip install --upgrade wyngthon

docs.title: Installing the Development Version
docs.text:
If you want the latest unreleased changes:

python3 -m pip install --upgrade https://github.com/P3dro-Im/Wyngthon/archive/refs/heads/main.zip

Warning

The development version may contain bugs and is not recommended for production use. However, when reporting a library bug, you should test against this version.

docs.title: Verifying the Installation
docs.text:
To make sure the library is installed correctly, run the following command:

python3 -c "import wyngthon; print(wyngthon.__version__)"

The library version should be displayed in the output.

docs.title: cryptg
docs.text:
If cryptg is installed, the library runs much faster because encryption and decryption are performed in C instead of Python. If your code deals with a large number of events or downloads/uploads many files, you will notice a significant speedup.

pip install cryptg

docs.title: Pillow
docs.text:
If pillow is installed, large images are automatically resized when sending photos to avoid the "invalid image" error.

pip install pillow

docs.title: aiohttp
docs.text:
If aiohttp is installed, the library will be able to download WebDocument media files.

pip install aiohttp

docs.title: hachoir
docs.text:
If hachoir is installed, metadata is extracted when sending files. Wyng uses this information to display the performer, artist, title, duration and size of videos.

pip install hachoir

docs.title: Installing Common Dependencies
docs.text:
If your system is apt-based, you can install the common dependencies with the following commands:

apt update
apt install clang lib{jpeg-turbo,webp}-dev python{,-dev} zlib-dev
pip install -U --user setuptools
pip install -U --user wyngthon cryptg pillow

docs.title: Installing Proxy Support
docs.text:
If you need to use a proxy to access Wyng, you must install the python-socks package:

pip install python-socks[asyncio]

Then pass the proxy to the client:

WyngClient('session_name', api_id, api_hash, proxy=proxy_config)

docs.title: ImportError
docs.text:
If you get the error ImportError: cannot import name 'WyngClient':

  1. Make sure your script is not named wyngthon.py
  2. Reinstall the library: pip install --upgrade wyngthon

docs.title: Dependency installation errors
docs.text:
If you have trouble installing dependencies:

pip install --upgrade setuptools wheel
pip install --upgrade wyngthon

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: A quick guide to getting started with Wyngthon. In this section you will learn how to create your first client and perform basic operations.

docs.title: Simple method (without API ID and Hash)
docs.text:
Wyngthon ships with default API credentials for Wyng, so you can create a client without obtaining your own keys:

from wyngthon import WyngClient, events, sync
from wyngthon.sessions import StringSession

# No api_id or api_hash needed
client = WyngClient(StringSession())
client.start()

docs.title: Standard method (with API ID and Hash)
docs.text:
For standard usage, you first need to obtain your API ID and Hash from my.telegram.org:

from wyngthon import WyngClient

api_id = 12345
api_hash = '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef'

# The first parameter is the session file name
with WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash) as client:
    client.loop.run_until_complete(client.send_message('me', 'Hello, myself!'))

Important

Avoid naming your script wyngthon.py! Python will try to import the client from that file and fail with an error.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
Here is a complete quick-start example:

from wyngthon import WyngClient

api_id = 12345
api_hash = '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef'
client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

async def main():
    # Get your own information
    me = await client.get_me()
    print(me.stringify())

    # Username
    username = me.username
    print(username)
    print(me.phone)

    # Print all conversations
    async for dialog in client.iter_dialogs():
        print(dialog.name, 'has ID', dialog.id)

    # Send a message to yourself
    await client.send_message('me', 'Hello, myself!')

    # Send a message to a chat
    await client.send_message(-100123456, 'Hello, group!')

    # Send a message to a contact
    await client.send_message('+989123456789', 'Hello, my friend!')

    # Send a message to a username
    await client.send_message('username', 'Testing Wyngthon!')

    # Send with formatting
    message = await client.send_message(
        'me',
        'This message has **bold**, `code`, __italic__ and '
        'a [beautiful website](https://example.com)!',
        link_preview=False
    )

    print(message.raw_text)
    await message.reply('Great!')

    # Send a file
    await client.send_file('me', '/home/me/Pictures/holidays.jpg')

    # Print message history
    async for message in client.iter_messages('me'):
        print(message.id, message.text)

        if message.photo:
            path = await message.download_media()
            print('File saved to', path)

with client:
    client.loop.run_until_complete(main())

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
Tip

Wyngthon is an asynchronous (async) library, so you need to work with asyncio. In general, write all of your code inside an async def function:

client = ...

async def do_something(me):
    ...

async def main():
    # Most of your code should go here
    me = await client.get_me()
    await do_something(me)

with client:
    client.loop.run_until_complete(main())

docs.title: The Entity Concept
docs.text: An Entity refers to any User, Chat, or Channel object that the API returns in response to certain methods, such as GetUsersRequest.

docs.title: What can be used as an Entity?
docs.text:
• Usernames: such as username
  • Phone numbers: such as +989123456789
  • Chat links: such as t.me/username
  • Invite links: such as t.me/joinchat/AAAAAFFszQPyPEZ7wgxLtd
  • IDs: such as 123456
  • The objects themselves: such as User, Chat, or Channel

docs.title: Order of preference for Entities
docs.text:
Use them from best to worst:

  1. Input Entities: such as event.input_chat or message.input_sender
  2. Entities: such as user or channel (if you already have them)
  3. IDs: the session cache is used
  4. Usernames, phone numbers, and links: the cache is used unless you call client.get_entity()

docs.title: The Session Concept
docs.text: A Session is an important part of the library that stores authentication information and the entity cache.

docs.title: Session types
docs.text:
1. SQLiteSession: The default. Data is stored in an SQLite file.
  2. MemorySession: Data is stored in memory.
  3. StringSession: Data is stored in memory but can be saved as a string.

docs.title: The session file
docs.text:
When you create WyngClient('anon'), an anon.session file is created in the current directory. This file contains:

  • The server IP address and port
  • The authorization key
  • Information about the entities you have seen
  • The access_hash of users and channels

docs.title: The Events Concept
docs.text: Events are used to receive notifications about new messages, members joining, typing, and more.

docs.title: Main event types
docs.text:
• NewMessage: A new message was received
  • MessageEdited: A message was edited
  • MessageDeleted: A message was deleted
  • CallbackQuery: An inline button was clicked
  • ChatAction: A new member joined or left
  • InlineQuery: An inline query was received
  • UserUpdate: A user's information changed

docs.title: Event usage example
docs.text:
from wyngthon import WyngClient, events

client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

@client.on(events.NewMessage)
async def my_event_handler(event):
    if 'hello' in event.raw_text:
        await event.reply('hi!')

client.start()
client.run_until_disconnected()

docs.title: Understanding Entities in Events
docs.text:
When you need the user or chat in which an event occurred, you must use the following methods:

async def handler(event):
    # Correct
    chat = await event.get_chat()
    sender = await event.get_sender()
    chat_id = event.chat_id
    sender_id = event.sender_id

    # Wrong - do not do this
    chat = event.chat
    sender = event.sender
    chat_id = event.chat.id
    sender_id = event.sender.id

Events are similar to messages, but they do not carry all of a message's information! When you fetch a message manually, it has all the necessary information. But when you receive an update about a message, it does not have all the information, so you must use methods, not properties.

from wyngthon import WyngClient

async def main():

    # Use await for asynchronous operations
    me = await client.get_me()

# Run the main loop
asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Mastering asyncio
docs.text: Wyngthon is built on top of asyncio. To use the library effectively, you need to understand the basic concepts of asyncio.

docs.title: What Is asyncio?
docs.text: asyncio is a Python standard library module that lets you write asynchronous code. It allows you to perform time-consuming operations (such as network requests) without blocking the main execution of your program.

docs.title: coroutine
docs.text:
An async def function is a coroutine:

async def my_function():
    print('Start')
    await some_async_operation()
    print('End')

docs.title: await
docs.text:
The await keyword waits for an asynchronous operation to finish:

async def main():
    result = await client.get_me()
    print(result.stringify())

docs.title: event loop
docs.text:
The event loop is responsible for running coroutines:

import asyncio

async def main():
    # Your code runs here
    pass

# Run the event loop
asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Basic Structure
docs.text:
import asyncio
from wyngthon import WyngClient

async def main():
    client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

    # Use await for asynchronous operations
    me = await client.get_me()
    print(me.stringify())

    # Run the event loop
    await client.run_until_disconnected()

# Run the main loop
asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Using a with Block
docs.text:
import asyncio
from wyngthon import WyngClient

async def main():
    with WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash) as client:
        me = await client.get_me()
        print(me.stringify())

        await client.run_until_disconnected()

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Using client.loop
docs.text:
from wyngthon import WyngClient

client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

async def main():
    me = await client.get_me()
    print(me.stringify())

    await client.run_until_disconnected()

with client:
    client.loop.run_until_complete(main())

docs.title: Sending Multiple Messages
docs.text:
import asyncio
from wyngthon import WyngClient

async def main():
    with WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash) as client:
        # Send several messages
        for i in range(5):
            await client.send_message('me', f'Message {i+1}')
            await asyncio.sleep(1)  # 1 second delay

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Receiving and Processing Messages
docs.text:
import asyncio
from wyngthon import WyngClient

async def main():
    with WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash) as client:
        async for message in client.iter_messages('me'):
            print(f'Message {message.id}: {message.text}')

            # Process messages concurrently
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Concurrent Event Handlers
docs.text:
import asyncio
from wyngthon import WyngClient, events

client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

@client.on(events.NewMessage(pattern=r'(?i)hi|hello'))
async def handler1(event):
    await event.reply('Hello! (from handler 1)')

@client.on(events.NewMessage(pattern=r'(?i)help'))
async def handler2(event):
    await event.reply('Help! (from handler 2)')

async def main():
    await client.start()
    await client.run_until_disconnected()

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: 1. Use await
docs.text:
All methods that work with the network must be called with await:

# Correct
me = await client.get_me()
await client.send_message('me', 'Hello')

# Wrong
me = client.get_me()  # Error!
client.send_message('me', 'Hello')  # Error!

docs.title: 2. Handlers must be async
docs.text:
Event handlers must be async def:

# Correct
@client.on(events.NewMessage)
async def handler(event):
    await event.reply('Reply')

# Wrong
@client.on(events.NewMessage)
def handler(event):
    event.reply('Reply')  # Error!

docs.title: 3. Use asyncio.sleep
docs.text:
To add a delay in asynchronous code, use asyncio.sleep:

import asyncio

# Correct
await asyncio.sleep(1)

# Wrong
import time
time.sleep(1)  # Blocks the event loop!

docs.title: 4. Use gather for concurrent operations
docs.text:
import asyncio

async def main():
    # Run several coroutines concurrently
    await asyncio.gather(
        client.send_message('user1', 'Hello 1'),
        client.send_message('user2', 'Hello 2'),
        client.send_message('user3', 'Hello 3')
    )

docs.title: The "This event loop is already running" Error
docs.text:
# Wrong
loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
loop.run_until_complete(main())

# Correct
asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: The "Cannot run the event loop while another loop is running" Error
docs.text:
# Wrong
async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    loop.run_until_complete(some_coroutine())

# Correct
async def main():
    await some_coroutine()

docs.title: A Blocked Event Loop
docs.text:
# Wrong
import time
async def main():
    time.sleep(1)  # Blocks the event loop!

# Correct
import asyncio
async def main():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # Does not block the event loop

docs.text: asyncio is a powerful tool for writing asynchronous code in Python. By understanding the basic concepts such as coroutine, await, and the event loop, you can use Wyngthon effectively.

docs.title: Bot API vs MTProto
docs.text: In this section we look at the differences between Bot API and MTProto (UserBot) so you can choose the best approach for your project.

docs.title: What Is the Bot API?
docs.text: The Bot API is the official Wyng interface for building bots. Bots are special accounts that are created and managed by other users.

docs.title: Advantages of the Bot API
docs.text:
• Simplicity: a simple API that is easy to use
  • Security: bots have built-in security restrictions
  • Official support: supported by Wyng
  • No user authentication required: only a Bot Token is needed

docs.title: Disadvantages of the Bot API
docs.text:
• Messaging restrictions: bots cannot message users unless the user messages them first
  • Sending limits: there are limits on the number of messages a bot can send
  • No access to full information: bots do not have access to all user information
  • Limited features: many features of the main API are not available in the Bot API

docs.title: What Is MTProto (UserBot)?
docs.text: MTProto is the core protocol of Wyng. With MTProto you can interact with the Wyng API as a regular user (UserBot).

docs.title: Advantages of MTProto
docs.text:
• Unlimited features: you have access to the entire Wyng API
  • Unlimited messaging: no restrictions on sending messages
  • Full access to information: all user and chat information is available
  • High flexibility: you can do anything

docs.title: Disadvantages of MTProto
docs.text:
• Complexity: the API is more complex
  • Requires an API ID and Hash: you must obtain them from my.telegram.org
  • Security risk: your account may be banned if used improperly
  • Session management required: you must manage the session and authentication

docs.title: Detailed Comparison
docs.text: Feature Bot API MTProto (UserBot) Account type Bot Regular user Message limits Limited Unlimited Access to information Limited Full API Simple Complex Requires user permission Yes No Security risk Low High Official support Yes No Requires an API ID No Yes Session management No Yes

docs.title: When to Use the Bot API
Suitable Use Cases
docs.text:
• Simple bots: bots that only reply to user messages
  • Notification bots: bots that send information to users
  • Service bots: bots that provide specific services
  • Small projects: projects that do not need complex features

docs.title: Bot API Example
docs.text:
from wyngthon import WyngClient

# Log in as a bot
bot = WyngClient('bot', api_id, api_hash)
await bot.start(bot_token='12345:0123456789abcdef')

@bot.on(events.NewMessage)
async def handler(event):
    if 'hello' in event.raw_text:
        await event.reply('Hello! I am a bot.')

await bot.run_until_disconnected()

docs.title: Suitable Use Cases
docs.text:
• UserBots: bots that work with your own user account
  • Automation scripts: scripts that perform repetitive tasks
  • Complex projects: projects that need the full API
  • Personal applications: applications you build for your own use

docs.title: MTProto (UserBot) Example
docs.text:
from wyngthon import WyngClient

# Log in as a user
client = WyngClient('user', api_id, api_hash)
await client.start()

@client.on(events.NewMessage)
async def handler(event):
    # Automatically reply to messages
    if 'hello' in event.raw_text:
        await event.reply('Hello! How can I help?')

await client.run_until_disconnected()

docs.title: Important Security Notes
docs.text:
Warning

Be careful when using a UserBot!

  • Never share your credentials
  • Do not use unknown scripts
  • Make sure your script does not violate Wyng's rules
  • Your account may be banned if used improperly

docs.title: Key Questions
docs.text:
1. Do you need full user information?

    • Yes → MTProto
    • No → Bot API

  2. Do you want to message users without them messaging you first?

    • Yes → MTProto
    • No → Bot API

  3. Is your project complex?

    • Yes → MTProto
    • No → Bot API

  4. Do you want to work with your own user account?

    • Yes → MTProto
    • No → Bot API

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
• Bot API is suitable for simple bots and small projects
  • MTProto is suitable for UserBots and complex projects
  • Each has its own advantages and disadvantages
  • Choosing the right approach depends on your project's needs

docs.title: Entity
docs.text: The library makes extensive use of the concept of an "Entity". An Entity refers to any User, Chat, or Channel object that the API may return in response to certain methods, such as GetUsersRequest.

docs.title: What is an Entity?
docs.text:
Many methods and requests need an Entity to work. For example, you send a message to an Entity, you get the username of an Entity, and so on.

Many things act as an Entity: usernames, phone numbers, chat links, invite links, IDs, and the types themselves. This means you can use any of them wherever an Entity is needed.

Note

Remember that a phone number must be in your contacts list before you can use it.

docs.title: Order of Preference for Entities
docs.text: Use them from best to worst:

docs.title: 1. Input Entities
docs.text:
For example, event.input_chat, message.input_sender, or caching an Entity that you use often:

entity = await client.get_input_entity(...)

docs.title: 2. Entities
docs.text:
If you already have the Entity, you can use it:

await client.send_message(user, 'Hello!')

docs.title: 3. IDs
docs.text: The Entity is always looked up in the cache (the *.session file caches the entities that have been seen).

docs.title: 4. Usernames, phone numbers, and links
docs.text: The cache is used here as well (unless you call client.get_entity()), but a network request may be sent if the username, phone number, or link has not been found yet.

docs.title: Getting Entities
docs.text:
With a Session, the library automatically remembers ID and hash pairs:

# (These examples assume you are inside an "async def")
#
# Dialogs are your open conversations.
# This method returns a list of Dialog objects that have an .entity property and other information.
#
# This is important because it populates the entity cache.
dialogs = await client.get_dialogs()

# All of these work and do the same thing
username = await client.get_entity('username')
username = await client.get_entity('t.me/username')
username = await client.get_entity('https://telegram.dog/username')

# Other kinds of Entity
channel = await client.get_entity('telegram.me/joinchat/AAAAAEkk2WdoDrB4-Q8-gg')
contact = await client.get_entity('+989123456789')
friend  = await client.get_entity(friend_id)

# Get an Entity by ID (User, Chat, or Channel)
entity = await client.get_entity(some_id)

# You can be more explicit about the type by wrapping it in a Peer
from wyngthon.tl.types import PeerUser, PeerChat, PeerChannel

my_user    = await client.get_entity(PeerUser(some_id))
my_chat    = await client.get_entity(PeerChat(some_id))
my_channel = await client.get_entity(PeerChannel(some_id))

Note

You do not need to fetch the Entity before using it! Let the library do its job. Use a phone number from your contacts, a username, an ID, or an input entity (preferred but not required), whichever you have.

docs.title: Peer and InputPeer
docs.text:
On top of the regular types, the API also uses Input* versions. The input version of an Entity (such as InputPeerUser, InputChat, etc.) only has the minimum information that Wyng needs to identify whom you are referring to: the ID and hash of a Peer.

The Entity ID is the same for all users and bot accounts, but the hash is different for each account, so do not try to use an access hash from one account in another account, because it will not work.

docs.title: Peers
docs.text:
Sometimes, Wyng only needs to know the type of the Entity along with its ID. For this purpose, there are also Peer versions of Entities that only have an ID. You cannot get the hash from them because you should not need it. The library has probably already cached it.

Peers are enough to identify an Entity, but they are not enough to make requests with. You need to know their hash before you can "use them", and to know the hash you must have "met" the Entity, whether in conversations, participants, forwarded messages, and so on.

Note

You can use Peers with the library. Behind the scenes, they are replaced with the input version. Peers are "not enough on their own", but the library does extra work to use the appropriate type.

docs.title: Input Entity vs Full Entity
docs.text:
As mentioned, API calls do not need to know all of an Entity's information, only its ID and hash. For this reason, the client.get_input_entity() method exists. It always uses the cache and, in most cases, does not send any API request.

When a request is sent, if you provide the full Entity (for example, a User), the library automatically converts it to the required InputPeer.

Always prefer client.get_input_entity() over client.get_entity()! Calling the latter always sends an API request to get the latest Entity information, but making requests only needs an InputPeer, not the full information. Only use client.get_entity() if you need actual information such as the username, name, title, and so on.

docs.title: Full Entity
docs.text:
In addition to PeerUser, InputPeerUser, and User (and their variants for chats and channels), there is also the concept of UserFull.

This full version has additional information, such as whether the user is blocked, notification settings, the user's bio or about text, and so on.

There is also messages.ChatFull, the equivalent of the full Entity for chats and channels, which also has the about section for channels.

You can get both by calling GetFullUser, GetFullChat, and GetFullChannel.

docs.title: Accessing Entities
docs.text:
When the documentation says "Bases: ChatGetter", it means the class you are looking at can also act as the class it is based on. In this case, ChatGetter knows how to get the chat that something belongs to.

# Message is a ChatGetter
message.is_private
message.chat_id
await message.get_chat()
# ...and so on

# SenderGetter is similar
message.user_id
await message.get_input_sender()
message.user
# ...and so on

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
TL;DR: if you are here because of "Could not find the input entity for", you should ask yourself, "How did I find this Entity through the official apps?" Now do the same thing with the library:

# (These examples assume you are inside an "async def")
async with client:
    # Does it have a username? Use it!
    entity = await client.get_entity(username)

    # Do you have an open conversation with them? Get the dialogs.
    await client.get_dialogs()

    # Are they a member of a group? Get the participants.
    await client.get_participants('username')

    # Is the Entity the original sender of a forwarded message? Get it.
    await client.get_messages('username', 100)

    # Now you can use the ID, anywhere!
    await client.send_message(123456, 'Hello!')

    entity = await client.get_entity(123456)
    print(entity)

Once the library has "seen" an Entity, you can use its numeric ID. You cannot use Entities that the library has not seen. The library must see them at least once and disconnect properly.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: Wyngthon has a powerful error handling system that lets you handle the various errors of the Wyng API.

docs.title: RPCError
docs.text:
These are the main errors of the Wyng API. They occur when your request runs into a problem.

from wyngthon.errors import RPCError, FloodWaitError, PeerFloodError

try:
    await client.send_message('username', 'Hello!')
except FloodWaitError as e:
    # Wait until the wait time is over
    print(f'Wait {e.seconds} seconds')
except PeerFloodError:
    # Message rate limit
    print('You have reached the message sending limit')
except RPCError as e:
    # Other API errors
    print(f'API error: {e}')

docs.title: FloodWaitError
docs.text:
When you send requests too quickly and have to wait:

from wyngthon.errors import FloodWaitError

try:
    await client.send_message('username', 'Hello!')
except FloodWaitError as e:
    print(f'Wait {e.seconds} seconds')
    # The library waits automatically
    # or you can wait manually
    import asyncio
    await asyncio.sleep(e.seconds)

docs.title: PeerFloodError
docs.text:
When you have reached the message sending limit:

from wyngthon.errors import PeerFloodError

try:
    await client.send_message('username', 'Hello!')
except PeerFloodError:
    print('You have reached the message sending limit. Please wait.')

docs.title: UserBannedInChannelError
docs.text:
When your account is banned in a channel:

from wyngthon.errors import UserBannedInChannelError

try:
    await client.send_message('channel', 'Hello!')
except UserBannedInChannelError:
    print('Your account is banned in this channel.')

docs.title: ChatWriteForbiddenError
docs.text:
When you don't have permission to write in the chat:

from wyngthon.errors import ChatWriteForbiddenError

try:
    await client.send_message('chat', 'Hello!')
except ChatWriteForbiddenError:
    print('You are not allowed to write in this chat.')

docs.title: UsernameNotOccupiedError
docs.text:
When the username doesn't exist:

from wyngthon.errors import UsernameNotOccupiedError

try:
    await client.send_message('nonexistent_username', 'Hello!')
except UsernameNotOccupiedError:
    print('The username does not exist.')

docs.title: UsernameInvalidError
docs.text:
When the username is invalid:

from wyngthon.errors import UsernameInvalidError

try:
    await client.send_message('invalid username!', 'Hello!')
except UsernameInvalidError:
    print('The username is invalid.')

docs.title: Using a general try/except
docs.text:
from wyngthon.errors import RPCError

async def safe_send_message(client, entity, message):
    try:
        await client.send_message(entity, message)
        return True
    except RPCError as e:
        print(f'Error sending message: {e}')
        return False
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'Unexpected error: {e}')
        return False

docs.title: Creating a decorator for error handling
docs.text:
from functools import wraps
from wyngthon.errors import RPCError

def handle_errors(func):
    @wraps(func)
    async def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        try:
            return await func(*args, **kwargs)
        except RPCError as e:
            print(f'RPC error: {e}')
            return None
        except Exception as e:
            print(f'Unexpected error: {e}')
            return None
    return wrapper

@handle_errors
async def send_message(client, entity, message):
    await client.send_message(entity, message)

docs.title: Using on_error
docs.text:
from wyngthon import WyngClient, events

client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

@client.on(events.NewMessage)
async def handler(event):
    await event.reply('Automatic reply')

# Handling errors in handlers
@client.on(events.NewMessage)
async def error_handler(event):
    try:
        # Risky operation
        await event.reply('Reply')
    except Exception as e:
        print(f'Error in handler: {e}')

docs.title: Using logging
docs.text:
import logging
from wyngthon import WyngClient, events

# Configure logging
logging.basicConfig(
    format='[%(levelname) %(asctime)s] %(name)s: %(message)s',
    level=logging.WARNING
)

client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

@client.on(events.NewMessage)
async def handler(event):
    try:
        await event.reply('Reply')
    except Exception as e:
        logging.error(f'Error in handler: {e}')
        raise  # Re-raise the error so it gets logged

docs.title: Sending a message with error handling
docs.text:
from wyngthon import WyngClient, events
from wyngthon.errors import FloodWaitError, PeerFloodError, RPCError

client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

async def send_with_retry(client, entity, message, max_retries=3):
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            await client.send_message(entity, message)
            return True
        except FloodWaitError as e:
            import asyncio
            await asyncio.sleep(e.seconds)
        except PeerFloodError:
            print('Message sending limit reached. Please wait.')
            return False
        except RPCError as e:
            print(f'Error on attempt {attempt + 1}: {e}')
            if attempt == max_retries - 1:
                return False
    return False

docs.title: A handler with error handling
docs.text:
@client.on(events.NewMessage(pattern=r'(?i)help'))
async def help_handler(event):
    try:
        await event.respond('Help: this is a help message.')
    except Exception as e:
        # If replying failed, stay silent
        pass

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
1. Always handle errors: especially FloodWaitError and PeerFloodError
  2. Use logging: for better troubleshooting
  3. Limit the number of retries: to avoid infinite loops
  4. Use a decorator for error handling: for cleaner code
  5. Don't re-raise errors: unless you want them handled at a higher level

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Events are an important topic in a messaging platform like Wyng. Ultimately, you want to be notified when a new message arrives, a new member joins, someone is typing, and so on. You can use events for this.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Let's start with an example of an automatic reply:

from wyngthon import WyngClient, events

client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

@client.on(events.NewMessage)
async def my_event_handler(event):
    if 'hello' in event.raw_text:
        await event.reply('hi!')

client.start()
client.run_until_disconnected()

This isn't much code, but some of it may be unclear. Let's break it down:

docs.title: Creating the client
docs.text:
from wyngthon import WyngClient, events

client = WyngClient('anon', api_id, api_hash)

Creation is the usual (passing the session name, API ID and hash, of course). Nothing we don't already know.

docs.title: The event decorator
docs.text:
@client.on(events.NewMessage)

This Python decorator attaches itself to the my_event_handler definition, and essentially means that on a NewMessage event, the callback function you are about to define will be called:

docs.title: The event handler
docs.text:
async def my_event_handler(event):
    if 'hello' in event.raw_text:
        await event.reply('hi!')

If a NewMessage event occurs and 'hello' is in the message text, we reply to the event with the message 'hi!'.

Note

Event handlers must be async def. After all, Wyngthon is an asynchronous library built on asyncio, an approach that is safer and often faster than threads.

You must await every method call that uses a network request, which is most of them.

docs.title: NewMessage
docs.text:
When a new message is received:

@client.on(events.NewMessage)
async def handler(event):
    print(event.raw_text)

docs.title: NewMessage with filters
docs.text:
Filtering outgoing messages:

@client.on(events.NewMessage(outgoing=True))
async def handler(event):
    # Only messages you have sent
    print(event.raw_text)

Filtering with regex:

@client.on(events.NewMessage(pattern=r'\.save'))
async def handler(event):
    # Only messages that start with ".save"
    if event.is_reply:
        replied = await event.get_reply_message()
        sender = replied.sender
        await client.download_profile_photo(sender)
        await event.respond('Your photo was saved {}'.format(sender.username))

docs.title: Accessing Entities in Events
docs.text:
When you need the user or chat in which the event occurred, you must use the following methods:

async def handler(event):
    # Correct
    chat = await event.get_chat()
    sender = await event.get_sender()
    chat_id = event.chat_id
    sender_id = event.sender_id

    # Wrong - don't do this
    chat = event.chat
    sender = event.sender
    chat_id = event.chat.id
    sender_id = event.sender.id

Events are like messages, but they don't have all of a message's information! When you fetch a message manually, it has all the necessary information. But when you receive an update about a message, it doesn't have all the information, so you must use methods, not properties.

                    level=logging.WARNING)

docs.title: Session
docs.text: Sessions are an important part of the library that store authentication information and the entity cache.

docs.title: What is a Session?
docs.text:
The first parameter you pass to the WyngClient constructor is session, and by default it is the session name (or full path). This means that if you create WyngClient('anon') and connect, an anon.session file is created in the current directory.

Note

If you pass a string, the file will be in the current working directory, although you can also pass absolute paths.

The session file has enough information to log in without sending the code again, so if you have to enter the code more than once, you may be changing the working directory, renaming or deleting the file, or using random names.

docs.title: Session File Contents
docs.text:
The database files, which use sqlite3, contain the information needed to communicate with Wyng servers, such as:

  • The server IP address and port
  • The authorization key (for encrypting messages)
  • Information about the entities you have seen
  • The access_hash of users and channels

docs.title: Entity cache
docs.text: By default, these files store all the input entities you have seen so that you can get user or channel information using only their ID. Wyng will not send the access_hash needed to retrieve more information if it thinks you have already seen them. This is why the library needs to store this information offline.

docs.title: Disabling entity storage
docs.text: If you do not intend to work with events, or you do not need to cache the access_hash associated with Entity IDs, you can disable this by setting client.session.save_entities = False.

docs.title: Session Storage Types
docs.text:
If you do not want to use the default SQLite Session storage, you can use one of the other implementations or your own.

Note

Although it is often not the case, SQLite may be slow enough to be noticeable, in which case you can use a different storage. Note that this is rare and most people will not have this problem.

docs.title: Available implementations
docs.text:
Wyngthon has three implementations of the abstract Session class:

from wyngthon.sessions import MemorySession, SQLiteSession, StringSession
  1. MemorySession: Stores session data in memory.
  2. SQLiteSession: Stores session data in an SQLite database on disk. The default.
  3. StringSession: Stores session data in memory, but can be saved as a string.

docs.title: Using StringSession
docs.text:
from wyngthon.sync import WyngClient
from wyngthon.sessions import StringSession

with WyngClient(StringSession(string), api_id, api_hash) as client:
    ...  # use the client

    # Save the session as a string
    string = client.session.save()

# You can also save any other type of session as a string
client = WyngClient('sqlite-session', api_id, api_hash)
string = StringSession.save(client.session)

docs.title: Creating Custom Storage
docs.text:
The easiest way to create your own custom storage implementation is to use MemorySession as the base and look at how SQLiteSession or one of the community implementations works.

You can find the relevant Python files in the sessions/ directory of the Wyngthon repository.

After creating your own implementation, you can add it to the list of community-maintained session implementations.

docs.title: String Sessions
docs.text: StringSession is a convenient way to embed login credentials directly in your code for very easy portability, since they only need a single string to log in without asking for a phone number and code (or to start faster if you use a bot token).

docs.title: Generating a String Session
docs.text:
The easiest way to generate a StringSession is as follows:

from wyngthon.sync import WyngClient
from wyngthon.sessions import StringSession

with WyngClient(StringSession(), api_id, api_hash) as client:
    print(client.session.save())

Think of this as a way to export your authorization key (what is needed to log in to your account). It prints a string to standard output (probably your terminal).

Warning

Keep this string safe! Anyone with this string can use it to log in to your account and do whatever they want.

This is similar to leaking *.session files online, but leaking a string is easier than leaking a file.

docs.title: Using a String Session
docs.text:
Once you have the string (which is a bit long), load it into your script somehow. You can use a regular text file and open(...).read(), or store it directly in a variable:

string = '1aaNk8EX-YRfwoRsebUkugFvht6DUPi_Q25UOCzOAqzc...'
with WyngClient(StringSession(string), api_id, api_hash) as client:
    client.loop.run_until_complete(client.send_message('me', 'Hello'))

These strings are really convenient for use in places like Heroku, because their ephemeral filesystem deletes external files after the program ends.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
1. Session safety: Session files are sensitive and should not be shared online.
  2. Renaming the file: If you rename or move the session file, you may have to log in again.
  3. Backups: Always back up your session files.
  4. StringSession: Suitable for deployment in cloud environments such as Heroku.

docs.title: Security Tips
docs.text:
Warning

Keep your String Session safe! Anyone with this string can use it to log in to your account and do whatever they want.

This is similar to leaking *.session files online, but leaking a string is easier than leaking a file.

docs.title: Important security tips
docs.text:
1. Never put a String Session in online source code
  2. Use environment variables to store the String Session
  3. Git-ignore text files that contain a String Session
  4. Use encryption to store the String Session
  5. Restrict access to files that contain a String Session

docs.title: Comparison with Other Methods
docs.text: Method Pros Cons SQLite Session Default, persistent Requires a file on disk String Session Highly portable Requires managing a string Memory Session Fast Data is kept in memory (temporary)

docs.title: Invalid String Session error
docs.text:
If you get an error such as "Invalid session":

  1. Make sure you copied the String Session correctly
  2. Make sure you are using the same original API ID and hash
  3. Generate the String Session again

docs.title: String Session doesn't work
docs.text:
If the String Session doesn't work:

  1. Make sure the String Session hasn't expired
  2. Make sure your account hasn't been banned
  3. Try again with a new String Session

    try:

docs.title: Word of Warning
docs.text: When using Wyngthon, it is important to be aware of Wyng's rules and limits so that your account does not get banned.

docs.title: 1. No Spam
docs.text:
• Never send promotional or spam messages
  • Never send messages in bulk
  • Never message users without their permission

docs.title: 2. Respect Privacy
docs.text:
• Never collect users' personal information without permission
  • Never share private information
  • Never enter private chats without permission

docs.title: 3. No Rule Violations
docs.text:
• Never use Wyngthon for illegal purposes
  • Never violate Wyng's rules
  • Never hack other people's accounts

docs.title: Message Sending Limits
docs.text:
• FloodWaitError: if you send messages too quickly, you have to wait
  • PeerFloodError: if you hit the message sending limit, you have to wait

docs.title: Request Limits
docs.text:
• Requests per second: a limit on the number of API requests
  • Requests per day: a limit on the total number of requests

docs.title: Account Limits
docs.text:
• Account ban: if you do not follow the rules, your account may be banned
  • Account restriction: if you do not respect the limits, your account may be restricted

docs.title: 1. Protecting Your Credentials
docs.text:
# Wrong - never expose credentials in your code
api_id = 12345
api_hash = '0123456789abcdef'

# Right - use environment variables
import os
api_id = int(os.environ.get('API_ID'))
api_hash = os.environ.get('API_HASH')

docs.title: 2. Protecting Your Session
docs.text:
# Wrong - never share your Session online
session_string = '1aaNk8EX-YRfwoRsebUkugFvht6DUPi_Q25UOCzOAqzc...'

# Right - use encryption

client = WyngClient('session', api_id, api_hash)
await client.start()

# Right - grant only the permissions that are needed

docs.title: 1. Use Error Handling
docs.text:
from wyngthon.errors import FloodWaitError, PeerFloodError, RPCError

async def safe_send(client, entity, message):
    try:
        await client.send_message(entity, message)
        return True
    except FloodWaitError as e:
        import asyncio
        await asyncio.sleep(e.seconds)
        return True
    except PeerFloodError:
        print('Message sending limit reached. Please wait.')
        return False
    except RPCError as e:
        print(f'Error: {e}')
        return False
